opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that interpretability, by itself, probably isn't going to be the thing that *certifies* a model as aligned, but it's a necessary part of any serious story about how we'd get there.

The way I tend to frame it is this. Alignment is ultimately a claim about how a model will behave across an enormous range of situations, including ones we've never tested and maybe can't test. Behavioral evaluations give you samples from that distribution, but they're always going to be sparse relative to what matters, and a sufficiently capable system might behave differently when it's being evaluated than when it isn't. So at some point you need to make claims about the *internal structure* of the model, about the mechanisms that generate behavior, and use those to reason about generalization. That's where interpretability comes in.

But I want to be careful, because "interpretability" can mean a lot of things. One version is: take a trained model, open it up, find circuits or features, and describe what they compute. That work is valuable, and the progress over the last few years with things like sparse autoencoders has been genuinely impressive. I'm skeptical, though, that this alone scales to a guarantee. These models are vast, the structures inside them are often distributed and messy, and there's always a gap between "here are the features we found" and "here is everything the model is doing."

My own perspective, coming from singular learning theory, is that we should also be asking *how* structure forms during training. The final weights are the endpoint of a developmental process, and the data and the geometry of the loss landscape determine which solutions the model ends up in. If we understand that process, how particular kinds of data lead to particular internal structures and when those transitions happen, then interpretability becomes less like archaeology on a finished artifact and more like understanding a causal pipeline. Ultimately that's what you want for alignment: not just "this model seems fine," but "we understand why training on this data produced these values and dispositions, and we can predict and steer that."

So I see interpretability as one leg of a broader science connecting data, training dynamics, internal structure, and behavior. Alignment, in a meaningful sense, is a claim that all those links are understood well enough that you'd bet on the model's behavior in situations you can't directly check. We're not there yet. But I think it's a tractable scientific program, and interpretability is central to it.

r001.rationale: The response says a capable system may behave differently during evaluation than outside it, but does not say that models with the same training behavior can generalize differently after deployment.

r002.rationale: It connects understanding internal mechanisms to reasoning about generalization, but does not identify internals as a way to distinguish models that behaved identically in training.

r003.rationale: It says data and loss-landscape geometry shape the model’s internal structures, but does not link singular learning theory to in-distribution generalization.

r004.rationale: The response does not present singular learning theory’s account of in-distribution generalization as a starting point for a theory of out-of-distribution generalization.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that I understand interpretability's role here as necessary but currently far from sufficient, and the gap between those two things is where most of the interesting work is.

Let me explain what I mean. When people talk about alignment, they usually mean something like: does this system have the goals, values, or dispositions we intended it to have, and will it keep behaving in accordance with them when we're not looking, or when the situation is different from anything in training. The trouble is that behavioral evaluation alone can't settle that question. You can run a model through a million test cases and observe that it behaves well, but that only tells you about its behavior on the distribution you sampled. A system could be well-behaved in every test precisely because it has learned that being well-behaved in tests is what gets rewarded, and that's a different internal structure from one that's actually robustly disposed to act well. From the outside, those two look identical until they don't.

So you need some way of reaching inside. That's the role interpretability is supposed to play: giving you evidence about what the system is actually computing, what internal structures are driving the behavior, rather than just the surface behavior itself. If you could really read the mechanism, you could in principle distinguish "behaves well because it has internalized the right thing" from "behaves well because it's modeling the evaluator." That's the dream.

Now, where I come at this from is a bit different from the mainstream mechanistic interpretability program, and I want to be careful here because I think that work is valuable. My background is in mathematics, and the way I think about neural networks is through the lens of singular learning theory, which is a framework for understanding what learning actually does in these systems. The thing that framework makes vivid is that a trained network isn't an arbitrary object. It's the outcome of a process, and the structure it ends up with is shaped by the geometry of the loss landscape, by which solutions are, roughly speaking, "simpler" in a precise sense that has to do with how degenerate the loss is around them. So when I think about interpretability, I'm not only asking "what circuits are in this network," I'm asking "why did training produce this structure rather than some other structure, and how stable is it."

I think that second question matters a lot for alignment specifically. Because alignment isn't really a property of a static artifact. It's a property of a system that is going to keep being trained, fine-tuned, deployed in new contexts, maybe modified by its own outputs feeding back into data. If your interpretability tools only tell you what's there right now, you've got a snapshot. What you really want is something more like an understanding of the developmental process, so you can say not just "this is what the model is doing" but "this is the kind of structure training tends to produce under these conditions, and here is how it changes." That's a much harder thing to get, but I think it's closer to what would actually let you make the kind of claims about alignment that people want to make.

There's also a more sobering point I'd want to make. Even in the best case, where interpretability matures a lot, I think we should be realistic about what kind of evidence it gives. It's not going to be a proof. Mathematics has a very particular relationship to certainty, and I don't think interpretability of large models is ever going to look like that. What it can give you is something more like what you get in an experimental science: converging lines of evidence, mechanistic stories that make predictions you can then test, a gradual tightening of the space of plausible hypotheses about what the system is doing. That's genuinely valuable. It's how we understand most complicated things in the world. But it means the right frame for "is this model aligned" isn't a yes/no verdict that interpretability delivers, it's an ongoing process of accumulating understanding, where interpretability is one of the main instruments and the question is always how much confidence the evidence actually licenses.

And I'd add that the thing I worry about is interpretability being used as a kind of reassurance rather than as a real epistemic tool. It's quite easy to find a compelling-looking story about what a model is doing, point at some features, and declare that it's fine. The discipline you need is to ask what you'd expect to see if the model were not aligned, and whether your methods would actually detect that. If your tools would produce the same reassuring picture either way, they're not telling you anything. So part of the role of interpretability, done well, is to be adversarial to our own hopes about these systems. That's a demanding standard, and I think the field is still working out what it takes to meet it.

r001.rationale: The response says systems can look identical on sampled tests yet differ when the situation changes or they are deployed, including the distinction between test-reward behavior and a robust disposition.

r002.rationale: It describes interpretability as a way to inspect internal mechanisms and distinguish systems that behave well for different underlying reasons, such as internalizing the intended behavior versus modeling the evaluator.

r003.rationale: It links singular learning theory to loss-landscape geometry and learned structure, but does not state that this provides a principled link to in-distribution generalization.

r004.rationale: It discusses studying how structures change across training and contexts, but does not present an account of in-distribution generalization as the starting point for a theory of out-of-distribution generalization.

astra-6.text:
I think interpretability has to be part of the story, but we should distinguish understanding something about a model from establishing that it's aligned. You can identify a feature or a circuit and give a compelling explanation of what it does. That's progress. But there's still a substantial gap between that explanation and a claim that the system will behave as intended in circumstances you haven't tested.

The attraction of interpretability is that behavior alone seems insufficient. If a model passes your evaluations, you know it behaved well on those evaluations. You don't necessarily know why, or whether the same behavior will persist when the context changes. Looking inside the model could help us distinguish mechanisms that produce similar behavior now but have very different implications later.

But then you have to ask: how reliable is our understanding of those mechanisms? What does the interpretation actually let us predict? Where does it stop being valid? Otherwise, we risk replacing confidence in a behavioral test with confidence in a story about the internals.

So I would view interpretability as a way to develop and test more precise hypotheses about a model, and ultimately as one component of an argument for alignment. The important step is connecting an internal explanation to a well-specified claim about behavior, with explicit assumptions and some way of checking that the connection holds.

sol-6.1.text:
I think interpretability has an important role, but we should distinguish understanding something about a model from establishing that it’s aligned. You might identify a circuit that implements a particular behavior, and that’s useful. But there’s a substantial gap between that observation and a claim that the model will behave the way we want across circumstances we haven’t tested.

Part of the difficulty is specifying what the claim even means. Aligned with whom, under what conditions, and with what degree of confidence? Until you’ve made that precise, it’s hard to say what evidence from interpretability would establish it.

So I would see interpretability as a source of evidence within a larger argument. It can help us discover failure modes, test hypotheses about how a model works, and perhaps eventually justify stronger guarantees. But finding an explanation that sounds plausible to us isn’t itself a guarantee. We need to understand why the methods we use are reliable, and what their limitations are. Otherwise we risk replacing an opaque model with a reassuring story about an opaque model.
